children: Chevron

is sticking to a 2027 target for a final investment decision on Yoyo-Yolanda, a gas field straddling the maritime border between Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, as the two governments negotiate the operating terms that must be settled before the US major can commit to spending.

The project appears with a 2027 investment decision in the table of major projects for 2025–2030 in Chevron’s investor presentation of November 5, Investir au Cameroun reported on November 20. The timetable is unchanged from the outlook Chevron presented at its investor day in November 2025, and the World Bank cited the same date in its November 4 economic report on Equatorial Guinea, the paper said.

Yoyo-Yolanda remains at the pre-front-end engineering and design (pre-FEED) stage, and none of the documents reviewed gives a date for first production, Business in Cameroon, its English-language sister publication, reported.

The fields hold an estimated 2.5 trillion cubic feet (about 70.5bn cubic metres) of gas, according to Cameroon’s Ministry of Mines. Joint studies allocate 84% of the resource to the Yoyo block on the Cameroonian side and 16% to the Yolanda block in Equatorial Guinea. Total investment has been estimated at $4bn, Business in Cameroon reported in February.
Operating agreement still under negotiation

The two countries signed a unitisation agreement on February 3 in Malabo, combining the separate Yoyo and Yolanda licences into a single unit. It built on a bilateral treaty signed in 2023, which opened the way for joint development of cross-border fields and which both parliaments had ratified and deposited with the United Nations by January 2025. The unitisation agreement sets the rules for developing the deposit jointly but does not commit anyone to building it.

The next step is a unit operating agreement with Chevron, which is still being negotiated. Delegations from Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea met in Yaoundé on November 4 to align their positions before a further round of talks with the company, Investir au Cameroun reported. In February, the two sides said discussions were continuing with the operator on the law that would apply to the production unit and on foreign-exchange rules.

Chevron holds the fields through Noble Energy Cameroon and Noble Energy EG, which it acquired with Noble Energy in 2020. Cameroon’s state hydrocarbons company, the Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures (SNH), holds a 25% stake in the Yoyo production-sharing contract, signed in 2017.

When the unitisation agreement was signed, Chevron tied the project to existing infrastructure in Equatorial Guinea. “The Yoyo-Yolanda project is central to Chevron’s strategy of supporting long-term liquefied natural gas supply and leveraging existing infrastructure at Alen and Punta Europa,” Jim Swartz, managing director for Chevron Nigeria and the mid-Africa region, said at the time, Reuters reported.

The development concept presented in February envisages a processing platform in the Yoyo area, three development wells and two export pipelines. Gas would then be processed separately at Bipaga in Cameroon and at Punta Europa on Equatorial Guinea’s Bioko Island. The concept remains a proposal that depends on further studies and the investment decision, Investir au Cameroun reported.
Gap left by
Hilli
For Cameroon, the project is the main prospect for new gas output after the departure of the
Hilli Episeyo
floating liquefaction vessel, operated by Golar LNG

, which left Kribi in August after eight years. The vessel produced about 10.8mn tonnes of LNG, loaded in 156 cargoes, from fields that SNH said had entered natural decline. SNH has identified Yoyo-Yolanda as its next major gas development, with resources far larger than the roughly 600bn cubic feet originally developed for
Hilli
, Business in Cameroon reported in July.
The World Bank’s 2026 economic update on Cameroon forecasts a rise in hydrocarbon exports in 2028 but does not explicitly link it to Yoyo-Yolanda, Investir au Cameroun noted.

Equatorial Guinea is further ahead with its own gas plans. Chevron took a final investment decision at the end of March on the $690mn Aseng gas project, which will tie the Aseng field back to the Alen platform and send its gas to the Punta Europa complex.

Chevron expects first gas from Aseng in 2028, Swartz said in October, Reuters reported. Malabo is counting on cross-border gas such as Yoyo-Yolanda to supply its Gas Mega Hub and keep Punta Europa running as its older fields decline.

title: Chevron keeps 2027 investment decision target for $4bn Yoyo-Yolanda gas project shared by Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea
